and the four courts of Central Java

died.note: Per court tradition.
The same article gives 1584 in its text.
Per court tradition (Babad Tanah Jawi: died of old age).
Some babad versions; others have him become a cleric (Sunan Parakan).

senapati.name: Senapati
senapati.title: Panembahan
senapati.bio: Founder of the Mataram kingdom, born Danang Sutawijaya, son of Ki Ageng Pemanahan and adopted son of Sultan Hadiwijaya of Pajang. Much of his story, including his bond with the sea goddess Nyai Roro Kidul, comes from later court chronicles.

hanyakrawati.name: Hanyakrawati
hanyakrawati.title: Panembahan
hanyakrawati.bio: Second ruler of Mataram, born Raden Mas Jolang, son of Senapati. He died in 1613 in an accident while hunting deer in the Krapyak forest, which gave him his posthumous name, Panembahan Seda ing Krapyak.

sources.where: infobox and text; dates cited there to Hadiwidjojo 1956

show.sub: daughter of Pangeran Benawa · per chronicles

martapura.name: Martapura
martapura.title: Adipati
martapura.bio: Son of Hanyakrawati by Ratu Tulungayu of Ponorogo. Tradition holds that he was enthroned for a single day in 1613, to keep a promise his father had made to his mother, before the throne passed to his half-brother, Sultan Agung.

agung.name: Agung
agung.title: Sultan
agung.bio: Mataram's most powerful ruler, born Raden Mas Jatmika (Rangsang). He took Madura and Surabaya, besieged Dutch Batavia without success in 1628–29, began the royal cemetery at Imogiri and is credited with the Javanese calendar. National Hero of Indonesia (1975).

sources.where: Pembunuhan dan penindasan, citing van Hoëvell 1849, p. 213

died.note: Killed with his family on Amangkurat I's orders. One article's 1672 confuses him with later lords of Surabaya.
Slain attacking the kraton.
The article places the attack in the context of 1647.

am1.name: Amangkurat I
am1.title: Susuhunan
am1.bio: Son of Sultan Agung, born Raden Mas Sayyidin. He moved the court to a brick palace at Plered and ruled harshly, ordering mass killings of religious scholars and their families after a 1648 revolt. Trunajaya's rebels took his court in 1677; he died while fleeing.

show.sub: daughter of Pangeran Pekik of Surabaya

died.note: The chart's date. No source opened in November 2026 gives it; probably de Graaf. A source is still needed.

sources.where: lead and infobox, citing de Graaf 1976, p. 81

died.note: Executed on Amangkurat II's orders. The article places Payak both in Bantul and in "East Java".

show.sub:
Balinese rebel, lord of
Pasuruan · not of the dynasty

died.note: The lead gives 5 December 1706, uncited.

am2.name: Amangkurat II
am2.title: Susuhunan
am2.bio: Born Raden Mas Rahmat, son of Amangkurat I. He won back the throne with VOC help after 1677, mortgaging north-coast lands to the Company, crushed Trunajaya and moved the court to Kartasura. He later sheltered the fugitive Untung Surapati, whom the Dutch wanted.

pb1.name: Pakubuwana I
pb1.title: Susuhunan
pb1.bio: Born Raden Mas Darajat and long known as Pangeran Puger, a son of Amangkurat I. He rose against his nephew Amangkurat III and, with VOC troops, took Kartasura in 1705, paying the Company with land on Madura and yearly rice deliveries.

am3.name: Amangkurat III
am3.title: Susuhunan
am3.bio: Born Raden Mas Sutikna, called Sunan Mas, son of Amangkurat II. His uncle Pangeran Puger, backed by the VOC, displaced him in the First Javanese War of Succession. He surrendered at Surabaya in 1708 and died in exile in Ceylon.

am4.name: Amangkurat IV
am4.title: Susuhunan
am4.bio: Born Raden Mas Suryaputra, son of Pakubuwana I, also called Sunan Jawi. His reign was taken up by the Second Javanese War of Succession (1719–23), in which his brothers and an uncle rose against him and the VOC backed him. He died in 1726, reportedly of poison.

pb2.name: Pakubuwana II
pb2.title: Susuhunan
pb2.bio: Born Raden Mas Prabasuyasa, son of Amangkurat IV; he came to the throne as a boy of about fifteen. His rule was broken in 1742–43, and the court later left Kartasura for the new palace at Surakarta. He was the last ruler of undivided Mataram.

died.note: After childbirth, per the article.

show.sub: daughter of Pangeran Blitar · per chronicles

pb3.name: Pakubuwana III
pb3.title: Susuhunan
pb3.bio: Born Raden Mas Suryadi, son of Pakubuwana II. Early in his reign Mataram was divided: the Treaty of Giyanti (1755) gave half the realm to Mangkubumi (Hamengkubuwana I), and the Treaty of Salatiga (1757) created the Mangkunegaran. First Susuhunan of Surakarta alone.

show.sub: queen · by one account a dancer

born.note: Ricklefs ("The Yasadipura Problem", 1997) doubts the Tus Pajang birth date.

sources.where: section "Yasadipura I and the Book of Cabolek", n. 24 (from Soebardi and the Tus Pajang)

died.note: Buried at Pengging.
Ricklefs' corrected year; AJ 1729 falls in 1802–1803.

sources.where: son and successor of Yasadipura I

pb4.name: Pakubuwana IV
pb4.title: Susuhunan
pb4.bio: Born Raden Mas Subadya, called Sunan Bagus. In 1790 VOC, Yogyakarta and Mangkunegaran forces surrounded his palace until he handed over the religious advisers they objected to, an episode known as the Pakepung. He is credited with the moral poem Serat Wulangreh.

pb5.name: Pakubuwana V
pb5.title: Susuhunan
pb5.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Sugandhi, son of Pakubuwana IV; reigned only 1820–1823. He was called Sunan Sugih, 'the wealthy', which Wikipedia explains by his generosity, such as paying his stepmother's funeral and debts.

pb7.name: Pakubuwana VII
pb7.title: Susuhunan
pb7.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Malik-i-Salikin, a son of Pakubuwana IV. He took the throne in 1830 when the Dutch removed his nephew Pakubuwana VI, and reigned until his death in 1858.
aka: Kanjeng Gusti Pangeran Adipati Harya Purbaya

pb8.name: Pakubuwana VIII
pb8.title: Susuhunan
pb8.bio: Born Raden Mas Kusen (also given as Kuseini), the eldest son of Pakubuwana IV by a concubine. He came to the throne at about 69 after his half-brother Pakubuwana VII, and his three-year reign was the shortest at Surakarta.

pb6.name: Pakubuwana VI
pb6.title: Susuhunan
pb6.bio: Born Raden Mas Sapardan, called Sinuhun Bangun Tapa for his ascetic practice. He is said to have secretly backed Diponegoro in the Java War; the Dutch deposed him in 1830 and exiled him to Ambon, where he died. National Hero of Indonesia (1964).

died.note: Dutch reports called it an accident; a 1957 exhumation is said to have found a bullet wound (unsourced in Wikipedia).

pb9.name: Pakubuwana IX
pb9.title: Susuhunan
pb9.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Duksina, son of the exiled Pakubuwana VI. Called Sinuhun Bangun Kedhaton for his rebuilding of the palace, he patronised letters; his court poet Ranggawarsita wrote the Serat Kalatidha in this reign.

pb10.name: Pakubuwana X
pb10.title: Susuhunan
pb10.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Sayyidin Malikul Kusna, son of Pakubuwana IX; he reigned 46 years, 1893–1939. He and his family were patrons of early Indonesian organisations such as Budi Utomo and Sarekat Islam, and he was later named a National Hero of Indonesia.
aka: Gusti Raden Mas Sayyidin Malikul Kusna

pb11.name: Pakubuwana XI
pb11.title: Susuhunan
pb11.bio: Born Raden Mas Antasena (also given as Ontoseno), son of Pakubuwana X. His reign, 1939–1945, ran through the Japanese occupation, when the court lost most of its assets; he died weeks before Indonesia declared independence.

died.note: Aged 86 per Hukumonline; the Wikipedia infobox says 85.

pb12.name: Pakubuwana XII
pb12.title: Susuhunan
pb12.bio: Born Raden Mas Suryo Guritno, he succeeded as a young man in 1945 and reigned 59 years. From 1946 Surakarta lost its special status and became a residency of Central Java, leaving the Susuhunan a ceremonial figure. Called Sinuhun Hamardika.

pb13.name: Pakubuwana XIII
pb13.title: Susuhunan
pb13.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Suryo Partono, known as Hangabehi. His accession in 2004 was disputed by his half-brother Tedjowulan, crowned by other siblings; they were reconciled in 2012. He died in November 2025, and his own succession is disputed between two sons.

born.note: Stated without a citation in both Wikipedias.

died.note: Date from news reports; the hospital is from Wikipedia only.

pb14p.name: Pakubuwana XIV
pb14p.title: Susuhunan
aka: Gusti Raden Mas Suryo Aryo Mustiko

hb1.name: Hamengkubuwana I
hb1.title: Sri Sultan
hb1.bio: Known before his accession as Pangeran Mangkubumi. He fought the VOC until the Treaty of Giyanti (1755) gave him half of Mataram, where he founded the Yogyakarta sultanate and laid out its palace and the Taman Sari water garden. National Hero of Indonesia (2006).

died.note: Buried at Imogiri.

hb2.name: Hamengkubuwana II
hb2.title: Sri Sultan
hb2.bio: Born Raden Mas Sundoro; called Sultan Sepuh after his removals. He defied Dutch and then British authority, and reigned three times: deposed in 1810 under Daendels, restored in 1811, deposed and exiled after the British stormed the palace in 1812, and restored in 1826 during the Java War.

hb3.name: Hamengkubuwana III
hb3.title: Sri Sultan
hb3.bio: Born Raden Mas Surojo, son of Hamengkubuwana II. He twice replaced his father: as regent from 1810 and as sultan under the British from 1812. That second accession cost Yogyakarta Kedu and other lands, its army, and land for the new Pakualaman.

sources.where: p. 190 of the scan (I = birth, II = accession, III = death)

hb4.name: Hamengkubuwana IV
hb4.title: Sri Sultan
hb4.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Ibnu Jarot, he became sultan aged about ten in 1814, with Paku Alam I governing for him. His own short rule was dominated by the chief minister Danureja IV and the Dutch. He died suddenly after an outing, hence the name Sultan Seda Besiyar.

hb5.name: Hamengkubuwana V
hb5.title: Sri Sultan
hb5.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Gatot Menol, he became sultan as a small child under a regency council. Set aside in 1826 for his great-grandfather Hamengkubuwana II during the Java War, he was restored in 1828, sought accommodation with the Dutch after the war, and patronised dance and letters.

hb6.name: Hamengkubuwana VI
hb6.title: Sri Sultan
hb6.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Mustojo and known as Pangeran Adipati Mangkubumi before his accession, he was chosen by the Dutch when Hamengkubuwana V died without a son. His marriage to a daughter of Pakubuwana VIII eased tension with Surakarta. A strong earthquake hit Yogyakarta in 1867.

hb7.name: Hamengkubuwana VII
hb7.title: Sri Sultan
hb7.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Murtejo, son of Hamengkubuwana VI. Called Sultan Sugih, 'the rich sultan', for the income his court drew from sugar mills, land leases and railway fees. He lent a building for Budi Utomo's first congress, and abdicated in January 1921.

hb8.name: Hamengkubuwana VIII
hb8.title: Sri Sultan
hb8.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Sujadi, he was recalled from study in the Netherlands to become sultan in 1921. He funded schools and health care, rebuilt much of the palace and the Great Mosque, and presided over a golden age of Yogyakarta dance and wayang wong.

sources.where: p. 193 of the scan, printed p. 153
p. 193 of the scan, printed p. 153

hb9.name: Hamengkubuwana IX
hb9.title: Sri Sultan
hb9.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Dorojatun. In 1945 he and Paku Alam VIII declared Yogyakarta part of the new Republic, which he helped fund from the palace treasury. Vice-President of Indonesia 1973–1978, father of Indonesian scouting, and National Hero (1990).

hb10.name: Hamengkubuwana X
hb10.title: Sri Sultan
hb10.bio: Born Bendara Raden Mas Herjuno Darpito, son of Hamengkubuwana IX. Sultan since 1989 and Governor of Yogyakarta since 1998. Royal decrees in 2015 changed his court title to Hamengku Bawono and named his eldest daughter heir; some of his brothers dispute the changes.
aka: Sri Sultan Hamengku Bawono Ingkang Jumeneng Kasepuluh

pa1.name: Paku Alam I
pa1.title: KGPAA
pa1.bio: Born Natakusuma, a son of Hamengkubuwana I. Rewarded for helping the British in the Yogyakarta conflict of 1812, he received a small hereditary principality, the Pakualaman, within the sultanate. He governed for the boy sultan Hamengkubuwana IV from 1814.

pa2.name: Paku Alam II
pa2.title: KGPAA
pa2.bio: Born Raden Tumenggung Natadiningrat, son of Paku Alam I; reigned 1829/30–1858. His court is remembered for its literature, with manuscripts such as Sestra Ageng Adidarma from his time.

sources.where: p. 194 of the scan, printed p. 154
p. 194 of the scan, printed p. 154

pa3.name: Paku Alam III
pa3.title: KGPAA
pa3.bio: Born Sasraningrat, son of Paku Alam II; reigned 1858–1864. He is credited with moral and religious writings including Serat Darmo Wirayat, and was buried at the old royal graves of Kotagede.
aka: Kanjeng Gusti Pangeran Adipati Surya Sasraningrat

pa4.name: Paku Alam IV
pa4.title: KGPAA
pa4.bio: Born Raden Mas Nataningrat, a nephew of Paku Alam III; reigned 1864–1878. Indonesian Wikipedia describes the duchy as in decline in his time. He was the last Paku Alam buried at Kotagede.
aka: Kanjeng Gusti Pangeran Adipati Surya Sasraningrat

pa5.name: Paku Alam V
pa5.title: KGPAA
pa5.bio: Born Raden Mas Natawijaya, he took over in 1878 but was allowed the title Paku Alam V only in 1883. He disbanded the Pakualaman troops in 1892, sent relatives to study in the Netherlands, and founded the Girigondo royal cemetery.

sources.where: p. 194 of the scan, printed p. 154

pa6.name: Paku Alam VI
pa6.title: KGPAA
pa6.bio: Born Raden Mas Natakusuma, son of Paku Alam V. Crowned in April 1901 and dead by June 1902, he had the shortest reign of any Paku Alam; a regency council governed until 1906.

pa7.name: Paku Alam VII
pa7.title: KGPAA
pa7.bio: Born Raden Mas Surarjo, son of Paku Alam VI; appointed in 1906 after a regency. He married a daughter of Pakubuwana X and worked with the colonial government on social and land reforms.

pa8.name: Paku Alam VIII
pa8.title: KGPAA
pa8.bio: Born Raden Mas Sularso Kunto Suratno, son of Paku Alam VII. In 1945 he joined Hamengkubuwana IX in bringing Yogyakarta into the Republic. First Vice-Governor of Yogyakarta from 1950, he was Governor from 1988 until his death in 1998.
aka: Gusti Raden Mas Sularso Kunto Suratno

pa9.name: Paku Alam IX
pa9.title: KGPAA
pa9.bio: Born Raden Mas Ambarkusumo, son of Paku Alam VIII. His succession in 1998 was disputed by his half-brother Anglingkusumo; he was formally installed in 1999 and served as Vice-Governor of Yogyakarta from 2002 until his death in 2015.

pa10.name: Paku Alam X
pa10.title: KGPAA
pa10.bio: Born Raden Mas Wijoseno Hario Bimo, eldest son of Paku Alam IX, and known as KGPH Suryodilogo before his accession in January 2016. Vice-Governor of Yogyakarta since May 2016. His accession was challenged by the side of Anglingkusumo, a rival claimant since 1998.

born.note: Year worked out from his age; no birth date was found in a source that could be opened.

mn1.name: Mangkunegara I
mn1.title: KGPAA
mn1.bio: Born Raden Mas Said and known as Pangeran Sambernyawa. He fought the VOC and the courts for some sixteen years, for a time alongside Mangkubumi, until the Treaty of Salatiga (1757) gave him his own principality, the Mangkunegaran. National Hero of Indonesia (1988).

born.note: Ricklefs' biography, cited by Wikipedia, is titled 'Soul Catcher: Java's Fiery Prince Mangkunagara I, 1726–95'.

died.note: The article's "Raden Ayu Matahati"; the name Rubiyah does not appear in it.

show.sub: daughter of Hamengkubuwana I · m. c. 1746, div. 1763

mn2.name: Mangkunegara II
mn2.title: KGPAA
mn2.bio: Born Raden Mas Sulama (one source gives Slamet), grandson and successor of Mangkunegara I. In 1808 he raised the Mangkunegaran Legion, a force of some 1,150 men that remained the principality's army.

sources.where: Early life, citing a source naming him Raden Mas Slamet

mn3.name: Mangkunegara III
mn3.title: KGPAA
mn3.bio: Born Raden Mas Sarengat, a grandson of Mangkunegara II through his mother. An officer of the Mangkunegaran Legion who fought in the Java War, he reigned 1835–1853 and brought up his cousin, the future Mangkunegara IV.

mn4.name: Mangkunegara IV
mn4.title: KGPAA
mn4.bio: Born Raden Mas Sudira. Remembered as the poet of the Serat Wedhatama and as a modernising ruler who built the Colomadu and Tasikmadu sugar mills and paid officials salaries instead of land grants.

dunuk.name: Dunuk
dunuk.title: GRAy.
aka: Kanjeng Bendara Raden Ayu Adipati Mangkunegara IV

born.note: Given in the Javanese era; the conversion to 1830/31 is mine.

mn5.name: Mangkunegara V
mn5.title: KGPAA
mn5.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Sunita, son of Mangkunegara IV. Falling sugar prices, cane disease and debt brought a financial crisis in his reign, and the Dutch placed the principality's finances under supervision. He died after an accident in a Wonogiri forest.

died.note: The article body ends his reign on 2 October 1896.

mn6.name: Mangkunegara VI
mn6.title: KGPAA
mn6.bio: Born Gusti Raden Mas Suyitno, a son of Mangkunegara IV, he succeeded his brother in 1896. He paid down the principality's debts and modernised court custom, then in 1916 became the only Mangkunegara to abdicate, moving to Surabaya.

mn7.name: Mangkunegara VII
mn7.title: KGPAA
mn7.bio: Born Raden Mas Surya Suprapta; he studied at Leiden. A leading patron of Javanese culture, he helped found the Java Instituut and in 1933 the Solosche Radio Vereeniging, described as the first radio station owned by Indonesians.

mn8.name: Mangkunegara VIII
mn8.title: KGPAA
mn8.bio: Son of Mangkunegara VII, he succeeded in 1944. He was Vice-Governor of the short-lived Special Region of Surakarta in 1945–46, later an honorary army major general and a member of parliament, and helped revive court dance.

died.note: Place from English Wikipedia's infobox only. Indonesian Wikipedia's 3 September 1987, in Jakarta, appears to be Mangkunegara IX's accession date.
Road accident.

mn9.name: Mangkunegara IX
mn9.title: KGPAA
mn9.bio: Born Gusti Pangeran Harya Sujiwakusuma, son of Mangkunegara VIII; he succeeded in 1987 and was crowned in January 1988. His first wife was Sukmawati Sukarnoputri, daughter of President Sukarno.

mn10.name: Mangkunegara X
mn10.title: KGPAA
mn10.bio: Born Bhre Cakrahutomo Wira Sudjiwo, son of Mangkunegara IX and Prisca Marina. A law graduate of the University of Indonesia, he was crowned in March 2022 at 24, and has promoted Javanese culture through digital media and tourism.

kgpaa.expansion: Kanjeng Gusti Pangeran Adipati Arya (…Anom for a crown prince)

n_pamanahan.text: Granted the land of Mataram by the Sultan of Pajang (traditionally 1556; settled in the 1570s).

n_senapati.text: Court tradition tells of his union with Ratu Kidul, queen of the Southern Ocean (legend).

n_martapura.text: The chronicles say he was enthroned for a single day before giving way to his half-brother; no other source records the reign.

n_agung.text: Besieged Dutch Batavia in 1628 and 1629. Took the title of Sultan in 1641. National Hero (1975).

n_juru.text: Senapati's uncle and strategist; Mataram's first patih. By tradition a descendant (great-granddaughter in most genealogies), Ratu Wetan of Batang, was Sultan Agung's queen.

n_benawa.text: His father Hadiwijaya (“Jaka Tingkir”) of Pajang adopted the young Senapati, who helped him oust Arya Pangiri (c. 1586–87); Benawa then ruled Pajang as Mataram's vassal. By tradition his daughter's son was Sultan Agung.

n_pekik.text: Of the old Surabaya royal line; Amangkurat I had him and his family killed in 1659.

n_alit_am1.text: Killed attacking the palace; the king then had 5,000–6,000 ulama and their families massacred (per the VOC envoy Van Goens).

n_ratumalang.text: On her death the king had dozens of palace women executed (VOC report); her tomb is at Gunung Kelir.

n_trunajaya.text: Grandson of Cakraningrat I of Madura and son-in-law of Raden Kajoran; took Plered in 1677. Amangkurat II killed him himself in 1680.

n_surapati.text: His men killed the VOC's Captain Tack at Kartasura (1686); he sheltered Amangkurat III.

n_am1.text: In 1677 Trunajaya's rebels sacked his capital at Plered; he died while fleeing.

n_ratupb.text: Sponsored the Islamic–Javanese Carita Sultan Iskandar and Kitab Usulbiyah (c. 1729–30) and guided the young Pakubuwana II.

n_purbaya_p.text: With his brother Pangeran Blitar he led the Second War of Succession against Amangkurat IV; exiled 1723.

n_yasadipura1.text: Traditionally credited with reworking the Serat Rama and Dewaruci; Pakubuwana IV offered him the post of patih, which he declined.

n_ranggawarsita.text: The last great court poet; his Serat Kalatidha named the “age of madness” (zaman edan).

n_djatikusumo.text: Son of Pakubuwana X; studied at Delft. National Hero (2002).

n_pb1.text: Prince Puger. Took the throne from his nephew with VOC help in the First War of Succession (1704–08).

n_am3.text: Exiled to Ceylon by the VOC in 1708. His first wife, Puger's daughter Raden Ayu Lembah, was executed for an affair (chronicles), which embittered him against her father.

n_am5.text: Grandson of Amangkurat III, crowned by Chinese and Javanese rebels who took Kartasura in 1742.

n_am4.text: Survived the Second War of Succession (1719–23) against his brothers and an uncle.

n_pb2.text: Moved the court to Surakarta in 1745. On his deathbed in 1749 he ceded the kingdom to the VOC.

n_kpa_mn.text: Exiled by the VOC in 1728 (Batavia, then Ceylon and the Cape of Good Hope); d. c. 1738, reportedly reburied at Imogiri.

n_hb1.text: Prince Mangkubumi. Proclaimed rival Susuhunan in 1749; the Treaty of Giyanti (1755) made him Sultan of half the kingdom. National Hero (2006).

n_mn1.text: Raden Mas Said, “Pangeran Sambernyawa”. The Treaty of Salatiga (1757) gave him part of Surakarta's lands. National Hero (1988).

n_mn2.text: Raised the Legiun Mangkunegaran (1808), a Napoleonic-style legion.

n_pa1.text: Sided with the British, who stormed Yogyakarta's palace in 1812, and was rewarded with the Pakualaman (1813), which had its own small army, the Pakualaman Legion.

n_diponegoro.text: Eldest son of Hamengkubuwana III by a secondary wife, RAy. Mangkarawati, and so not in line for the throne. National Hero (1973).

n_pb6.text: Exiled to Ambon in 1830, suspected of backing Diponegoro. National Hero (1964).

n_ratuageng.text: Raised her great-grandson Diponegoro at Tegalrejo; credited with training the palace's female guard. Mother of Hamengkubuwana II.

n_ronggo.text: Rose against Governor-General Daendels and was killed in 1810, a prelude to the Java War.

n_sentot.text: Son of Ronggo by a secondary wife; surrendered in 1829.

n_kyaimaja.text: Son of Hamengkubuwana III's sister; died in exile in Minahasa, 1849.

n_ratuibu.text: Daughter of the patih Danureja II and GKR Hangger, a daughter of Hamengkubuwana II; mother of Hamengkubuwana V and VI.

n_gustiahmad.text: Born 13 days after his father's death in 1855; his uncle took the throne, and he died in exile in Manado.

n_juminah.text: Hamengkubuwana VII named three crown princes before Hamengkubuwana VIII; Juminah, invested in 1893, was removed, officially on grounds of health.

n_hb7.text: Known as “Sultan Sugih”, the rich Sultan: 17 sugar mills were founded in his reign. His sons, among them Tejokusumo, founded Krida Beksa Wirama (1918), the first dance school outside the palace.

n_norma.text: Married 1976; she lived 1930–2015. His companion during his vice-presidency.

n_hb5.text: Put on the throne as a child; set aside 1826–28 while the Dutch restored Hamengkubuwana II.

n_mn4.text: Mangkunegara IV wrote the Serat Wedhatama; his Puspawarna flew on the Voyager Golden Record (1977). He founded the Colomadu (1861) and Tasikmadu (1871) sugar mills.

n_nurul.text: Danced at Princess Juliana's wedding (1937); turned down Sukarno, Sjahrir and Hamengkubuwana IX; married her cousin, Lt. Col. Sujarso Surjosurarso, in 1954.

n_pb11.text: The Dutch chose him over Kusumayuda, the son Pakubuwana X preferred.

n_mn7.text: Studied at Leiden; co-founded SRV (1933), the first Indonesian-owned radio station.

n_mn8.text: Recognised by Sukarno in 1945 as head of a special region beside the Sunan's; its suspension in June 1946 ended Mangkunegaran self-rule.

n_pa8.text: Deputy Governor of Yogyakarta 1950–88, then acting Governor until his death in 1998. National Hero (2022).

n_hb9.text: Hosted the Republic's capital in Yogyakarta (1946–49). Yogyakarta became a Special Region in 1950 with the Sultan as Governor. Vice President of Indonesia 1973–78. National Hero (1990).

n_pb12.text: Surakarta's special-region status was suspended in 1946; it was folded into Central Java in 1950. It has since been a ceremonial court.

n_mooryati.text: Deputy Speaker of the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), 2004–09.

n_rubiyah.text: By tradition a cleric's daughter from Matah, near Nglaroh, who led Raden Mas Said's corps of women soldiers; a woman soldier of his court kept a diary of court life, 1781–91.

n_wulan.text: Mother of Mangkunegara I; sources differ on her father's line.

n_blitar_p.text: Son of Pakubuwana I; led the 1719 revolt with his brother Purbaya.

n_suyono.text: The Dutch refused him as heir, and Mangkunegara VI abdicated in 1916, the only Mangkunegara to abdicate.

n_abubakar.text: A grandson of Sultan Ismail of Johor: a royal marriage across the Strait.

n_hayu_pa2.text: Aunt of Diponegoro; mother of Paku Alam III and grandmother of Paku Alam IV.

n_suryopranoto.text: Led Sarekat Islam strikes and founded the sugar workers' union; Ki Hajar's elder brother.

n_nyihajar.text: Born Sutartinah, daughter of KPH Sasraningrat, a son of Paku Alam III, and so Ki Hajar's cousin; shared his Dutch exile, 1913–19.

n_notosoeroto.text: Dutch-language poet; co-founded the Indische Vereeniging (later Perhimpunan Indonesia); secretary to his friend Mangkunegara VII.

n_kihajar.text: Founded Taman Siswa (1922); first Minister of Education. National Hero (1959).

n_mangkubumi.text: In 2015 the Sultan issued decrees changing his own title, dropping the Islamic, male “Khalifatullah”, and renaming her Mangkubumi, the traditional name of the crown prince. This was widely read as naming her heir, though she has not been formally installed.

n_anglingkusumo.text: Son of Paku Alam VIII by Ratnaningrum, the wife ranked senior; proclaimed rival Paku Alam IX in 2012, after his elder brother Probokusumo's 1998 candidacy failed. Founded the Mangkualaman in 2021.

n_wiroyudho.text: The Mangkualaman is a self-proclaimed court with no recognition from the Indonesian state.

n_pb14p.text: Purbaya, crown prince since 2022, proclaimed himself on 5 Nov 2025 and was crowned on 15 Nov. His elder half-brother Hangabehi, named by a family council backed by the court's customary council on 13 Nov 2025, was crowned on 5 Sep 2026. Unresolved. The two are half-brothers: Purbaya by the queen, Hangabehi by a divorced wife.

n_prabukusumo.text: The Sultan's brothers rejected the 2015 decrees as contrary to palace custom (paugeran), which passes the throne to a son. In 2020 he removed Prabukusumo and Yudhaningrat from their palace posts.

n_tedjowulan.text: Since January 2026 the government-appointed custodian of the palace heritage site (Culture Ministry decree 8/2026); has not endorsed either claimant to Pakubuwana XIV.

n_mn10.text: Chosen in 2022 over his elder half-brother Paundrakarna, a grandson of Sukarno.

panels.intro: Founded in the 16th century, the Sultanate of Mataram came to rule most of Java. Civil wars and European intervention between 1755 and 1813 split it into four royal houses that survive today: the Surakarta Sunanate and the Mangkunegaran in Solo, and the Yogyakarta Sultanate and the Pakualaman in Yogyakarta.
caveats: Notes on uncertain points. The ancestry before Pamanahan, back to Brawijaya V of Majapahit, follows the Babad Tanah Jawi and is legendary. Dates before 1613 are traditional, from court chronicles compiled mostly in the 18th century (alternatives include 1582 or 1586/87 for the kingdom's founding and 1575 or 1584 for Pamanahan's death); Mataram rulers appear in Dutch VOC records from 1613–14 (de Graaf; Ricklefs). Only Sultan Agung used the title Sultan, from 1641; his successors were styled Susuhunan. Mataram used no fixed heraldic emblem; the red flag often shown for it appears to derive from 18th-century Dutch flag charts, where it is labelled Japara. The courts' emblems date from the 19th and 20th centuries.

Paku Alam reigns are dated from formal installation; Paku Alam I was appointed de facto on 29 June 1812, and a regency council ran the Pakualaman 1902–06. Nataningprang is also styled GPH or GRMH (Gusti Raden Mas Harya); he died before his father (d. 1858) and so never succeeded.

Getas Pandawa is also spelled Getas Pendawa, Bondan Kejawan Bondan Kajawan, Enis Anis, Pandansari Wandansari and Blitar Balitar. Crowns count reigns within each court: Surakarta's from Pakubuwana III (the court itself counts Pakubuwana II, who moved to Surakarta in 1745, as its first Sunan), and Hamengkubuwana III's regency of 1810–11 is counted as a reign. Hamengkubuwana IV's death is dated 1822 (some sources 1823). Prabu Hamijaya is also spelled Prabu Amijaya. Bendara's marriage is dated 1746 or 1747. KPA Mangkunegara's exile route and death date vary between sources.
Tien Suharto's descent from Mangkunegara III runs through her mother (she is often called his canggah, great-great-grandchild); the line is not fully documented.

Pakubuwana XII never named a queen, so no son had a clear claim, and the succession split in 2004. The Surakarta succession has been disputed since November 2025; a January 2026 court order concerns only Purbaya's civil-registry name and does not decide the succession (a challenge to it was ruled inadmissible on procedural grounds in July 2026; no appeal outcome has been reported). The Mangkualaman has no state recognition, and its dates (2021–22) vary between sources.
sources: Sources. Reign dates follow the courts' chronologies; early dates vary by source. Portraits: Wikimedia Commons (Tropenmuseum, KITLV, Rijksmuseum, Kraton Yogyakarta and Surakarta collections; CC BY, CC BY-SA and public domain), Pemda DIY
; early Mataram rulers are later artistic depictions. Emblems: Wikimedia Commons (Gunawan Kartapranata, RaFaDa20631; CC BY-SA)
. Maps: geoBoundaries (CC BY 3.0 IGO); historical extents after Ricklefs, Cribb and Hakim. Full picture credits:

maps.title: c. 1640 · Mataram at its height
maps.caption: Sultan Agung held Central and East Java and Madura; Cirebon and the Priangan were vassals. Blambangan, conquered 1639–40, was never firmly held. Banten, Batavia and the empty land between them stayed outside.

maps.title: 1743–49 · The coast lost
maps.caption: To regain his throne after the Chinese War, Pakubuwana II ceded the north coast and Madura to the VOC (1743, 1746). His 1749 cession of the whole realm stayed on paper while the interior was in revolt.

maps.title: 1755–57 · Giyanti and Salatiga
maps.caption: Surakarta and Yogyakarta split the kingdom, their lands interlocking field by field; the Mangkunegaran was carved out of Surakarta's share.

maps.title: 1812–13 · British rule
maps.caption: The British annexed Kedu and other districts and created the Pakualaman, whose scattered lands were later gathered in Yogyakarta's south-west. The box marks the detail maps.
maps.note: Drawn on modern regency boundaries; before 1830 the courts' lands were intermixed field by field, so earlier extents are approximate.

maps.title: 1830–1942 · After the Java War (detail)
maps.caption: The Dutch annexed the outer provinces, leaving the four courts only the Vorstenlanden around Surakarta and Yogyakarta, with a few enclaves (outlined).

maps.title: Since 1950 · In the Republic (detail)
maps.caption: Yogyakarta and the Pakualaman form the Special Region of Yogyakarta; the former Surakarta and Mangkunegaran lands are part of Central Java. The enclaves joined their surroundings (formally 1958).

split.title: How Mataram split
split.summary: From one kingdom to four courts

steps.title: One kingdom, four courts
steps.caption: Founded in the 16th century, the Sultanate of Mataram came to rule most of Java. Between 1755 and 1813, civil wars and European intervention split it into four royal houses that survive today.

steps.title: Mataram at its height
steps.caption: Panembahan Senapati founded the kingdom. Under his grandson Sultan Agung (r. 1613–1645) it held Central and East Java and Madura. Agung besieged Dutch Batavia in 1628 and 1629.

steps.title: The map around 1640
steps.caption: Agung's realm at its widest. Cirebon and the Priangan were vassals; Banten and Batavia stayed outside.

steps.title: Rebellion
steps.caption: In 1677 the Madurese rebel Trunajaya sacked Amangkurat I's capital at Plered; the king died while fleeing. His son Amangkurat II killed Trunajaya himself in 1680.

steps.title: Wars of succession
steps.caption: Prince Puger took the throne from his nephew Amangkurat III with the help of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) in the First War of Succession, 1704–08, and reigned as Pakubuwana I. Amangkurat III was exiled to Ceylon. A second war followed in 1719–23, when Pakubuwana I's sons rose against their brother Amangkurat IV.

steps.title: The coast lost
steps.caption: In 1742 rebels took Kartasura and crowned Amangkurat V. To regain his throne, Pakubuwana II ceded the north coast and Madura to the VOC; he moved the court to Surakarta in 1745, and on his deathbed in 1749 ceded the whole kingdom to the VOC, a cession that stayed on paper while the interior was in revolt.

steps.title: Giyanti, 1755
steps.caption: Prince Mangkubumi had proclaimed himself a rival Susuhunan in 1749. The Treaty of Giyanti made him Sultan of half the kingdom, as Hamengkubuwana I of Yogyakarta; Surakarta kept the other half under Pakubuwana III.

steps.title: Salatiga, 1757
steps.caption: Raden Mas Said, “Pangeran Sambernyawa”, received part of Surakarta's lands by the Treaty of Salatiga and became Mangkunegara I. That made three courts.

steps.title: Interlocking lands
steps.caption: Surakarta and Yogyakarta split the kingdom with their lands interlocking field by field; the Mangkunegaran was carved out of Surakarta's share.

steps.title: British rule and the fourth court
steps.caption: The British stormed Yogyakarta's palace in 1812. Paku Alam I had sided with them and was rewarded in 1813 with the Pakualaman, which had its own small army.

steps.title: The four courts today
steps.caption: Yogyakarta and the Pakualaman form the Special Region of Yogyakarta; the former Surakarta and Mangkunegaran lands are part of Central Java. All four courts survive, and Surakarta's succession has been disputed since 2025.
